title: UK financial regulators set out what boards should know about cyber resilience
summary: The UK financial regulators opened a consultation on 19 November about how firms demonstrate that essential services can continue or recover during a cyber incident. The Bank, PRA and FCA drew together expectations under the existing operational resilience framework and lessons from supervision. The release applies to firms already in scope of those requirements. Its emphasis is on governance, preparation and evidence that arrangements work. A firm’s board cannot infer compliance from adopting a specific product, and the consultation did not create a new binding obligation on the date it opened. Responses were requested by 26 February 2027, with final guidance expected the following year.

The regulators presented three different kinds of evidence for their concern. In the Bank’s Systemic Risk Survey, cyber risk featured among the developments respondents thought could have the greatest effect on the financial system. October had the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in five years, 52% above the preceding 18-month peak in May 2025. Separately, 88% of respondents to a Bank and FCA survey expected frontier AI capabilities to have a moderate or high effect on their risk profile over the next two years. The 52% figure compares reported incident counts. The 88% figure records expectations. Neither measures losses or the probability of disruption at any individual institution.

The consultation describes a chain of responsibilities that starts with the board and senior management. Firms are asked to establish clear accountability and risk appetite, understand the assets, information and external services essential to their operations, and provide regular reporting and assurance. Good internal reporting should help the board see which business services depend on an outside provider and whether recovery has been demonstrated. A report confined to spending totals or the number of controls installed gives limited insight into whether the firm can restore a service used by customers.

The release also puts incident response and recovery alongside prevention. It describes arrangements for identifying disruptions, containing their effects, restoring services and incorporating lessons from experience. The concern for investors and customers is the interruption to a financial service and the ability to recover, even when the immediate source of disruption lies outside the institution. A bank could have resources to strengthen its own systems yet still depend on a supplier to restore access to essential information. The release offers no performance scores for individual firms, estimates of sector losses or rankings of providers.

The regulators published separate material on effective practices relating to AI and quantum computing. Those documents were available for feedback on their usefulness but were outside the formal consultation. They give firms ways to consider emerging risks as technology changes. The statement separately reports that 64% of respondents to the Bank and FCA survey identified vulnerability management and patching as the area receiving the greatest increase in management attention owing to frontier AI. Extra management attention indicates a change of priorities. A board still needs evidence that the resulting work improved continuity of the services for which it is responsible. That evidence, and the scope of the eventual final guidance, would help determine the effect on firm expenditure.

questions.question: Which important service would take the longest to restore after a severe disruption?
questions.detail: The consultation calls for governance and assurance, while the release supplies sector-wide indicators rather than firm-level recovery evidence. For a creditor assessing operational exposure, ask for test results covering the service end to end, including the dependencies outside the institution. Compare the observed recovery time and customer impact with the board’s approved limits, then check whether deficiencies found in the exercise were actually closed.

questions.question: Does the rise in reported incidents imply higher expected losses for this firm?
questions.detail: October’s count compares reports received by the FCA with an earlier peak. The release supplies no consistent measure of severity, duration or financial damage. Before adjusting an insurance or earnings estimate, compare like-for-like incident reports with information on affected services, recovery costs and customers. Distinguish any change in reporting practice from a rise in serious disruption and keep survey perceptions separate from realised outcomes.

questions.question: Which governance changes should the firm prioritise while the guidance is still being considered?
questions.detail: The consultation and the two effective-practices publications have different status. A board deciding on expenditure should map current obligations and known service weaknesses against the proposals, identify accountable executives and document the evidence behind its choices. The final guidance, the regulator’s response to consultation and subsequent assurance results will show which changes are expected and whether they improved resilience in practice.

limitation: The figures concern reported events and survey responses. The separate AI and quantum publications were outside formal consultation, and the release contains no institution-level loss estimate.
